vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: a paper that parents sign to say their child can go
to give something of yours to somebody for a short time
a page of school exercises that a student fills in
very happy about something good that you or somebody did
a person who is in the same class as you
a small object you keep because it reminds you of a person
to give your finished work to the teacher
to take something of somebody else's and give it back later
to be somebody's, to be their property
a school visit to a place outside the school

paras: Dear Grade 4 families, this month our class is opening a museum, and you are part of it. Every child is bringing one object from home that belongs to somebody in the family: a grandparent's watch, a mother's first camera, an uncle's old map. The only rule is that the object has a story, and the child can tell it.

Last week we had our first visitors. Lucas brought his grandfather's pocket watch, and he explained that it stopped in 1985 and nobody ever fixed it. Ana's object was a recipe book. It is her grandmother's, and the pages are full of notes in three languages. Ana's classmates wanted to know whose handwriting it was, and the answer was: everybody's. Her mother, her aunts and her grandmother all wrote in it.

Please do not send anything valuable. A keepsake is not the same as a treasure. A ticket from a trip, a postcard or a child's first shoe tells a better story than a gold ring. If the object is very special, take a photo of it and send the photo instead. The objects stay in our classroom for two weeks, on a shelf with each child's name, and then they go home in a closed bag.

Two practical notes. First, the worksheet about the object is due next Friday. Your child writes it, but please read it together: whose object is it, where is it from, and why is it important to your family? Second, our field trip to the city museum is on Thursday the 20th. Please sign the permission slip and send it back by Monday. The children are very proud of their museum, and we hope you can come and visit it on the last Friday of the month.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, in the style of a bilingual school newsletter.

items.situation: A teacher holds up a blue jacket after class. Ask whose it is.
tips: Whose plus the thing: whose jacket, whose bag.

items.situation: The jacket is your daughter's. Say it in two ways.
tips: Hers, never her's: no apostrophe on hers, ours or theirs.

items.situation: Say where your daughters' rooms are, in one sentence.
tips: The girls' rooms are upstairs, next to ours.
Two girls: the apostrophe goes after the s.

items.situation: A classmate wants to borrow a pencil. Your daughter says it is not hers. What does she say?
tips: Sorry, it isn't mine. It's my friend's.
Mine, yours, his, hers: the word replaces the thing.

items.situation: Tell the teacher about a family keepsake, and whose it was.
tips: We have my grandfather's watch. It was his, and now it's my mother's.
The person, then 's, then the thing.

items.situation: Ask another mother about her son's project.
tips: What is your son's object for the museum?
Your son's object, not the object of your son.

listenings.text: Hello, this is Mrs. Carter, the Grade 4 teacher. I am calling all the families today, because our lost and found box is full again. Here is what is in it. There is a blue jacket with no name. It is a small size, so it is probably a girl's or a younger boy's. There are two water bottles, a green one and a pink one. The pink one has the letters S and P on it, so if those are your daughter's initials, it is probably hers. There is also a lunch box with a cartoon cat on it, and a library book. The book is not a child's, it is the school's, so please look in your children's bags tonight and see if one of their books is missing. Everything stays in the box until Friday. After that, the clothes go to a charity, and the library book goes back to the library. Thank you, and have a good week.

My son's class is doing a family museum this month, and every child has to bring an object that belongs to somebody in the family. We looked everywhere. My wife's family keeps everything, so her parents' house was the obvious place. In the end my son chose my father's old camera. It isn't mine and it isn't his. Technically it is my mother's now, because my father gave it to her before he retired. My son's job was to find out the story, so on Sunday he called his grandparents. It turns out my father bought the camera on his first trip abroad, and he took every family photo with it for thirty years, including our wedding photos. My son wrote all of that on his worksheet. Then his teacher asked whose idea it was, and he said: mine. Which is true. I only drove.
